title: Campaign money from each lobbyist’s circle
question: How much reaches officials’ own campaign committees from registered lobbyists, their colleagues, their clients and the clients’ officers, firm by firm?
finding: Campaign filings since 2010 show $1.2 million in 2,925 contributions to the committees of City officials and candidates from lobbyists’ circles: $264,180 from registered lobbyists themselves, $225,225 from other people at lobbying firms and the firms, $114,028 from clients’ own funds and $570,279 from clients’ officers. Registered lobbyists made 635 contributions ($210,673) to City-office committees before the 2018 ban and 57 ($14,286) after it, 15 of the later ones to an official their firm reported contacting within two years. Lobbyists’ own reports list 205 contributions since 2018 ($124,975), 169 of them to City-office committees.
how: Every itemized contribution (Schedules A and C) to a committee controlled by a City official or candidate is tested against the lobbyist file. A giver counts as a registered lobbyist when surname and first name match a lobbyist active within a year and the employer written on the contribution is that lobbyist’s firm (or the occupation says lobbyist); as a colleague when the employer is a firm that sells lobbying; as a client’s officer when the employer is a client active within a year and the occupation is an owner, partner or senior officer title; and as the firm or client itself when the contributor is that organization. A client’s giving is shown under each firm it was paying at the time, so firm rows overlap and do not add up to the total. “Listed on lobbyists’ reports” is what lobbyists themselves reported giving or delivering with someone else named as the source of funds; it overlaps the committee filings and is never added to them. The ban date is the one used in the “lobby triangle” results, which lists the lobbyist-by-lobbyist cases.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. Since 2018 a registered lobbyist may not give to an official the lobbyist is registered to lobby; a contribution after that date to another office, to a party-committee seat or before the lobbyist registered for that agency is not covered, and the filings do not say which agencies a lobbyist was registered for. A further 2,699 contributions came from people who share a lobbyist’s name but give another employer; they are not counted. The employer on a contribution is self-reported. Law firms and large companies have many staff who give for their own reasons. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for.
